thread.title_full: Dallas mechanic exposes massive roofing scheme, police take the case - NewsBreak

author: Dave Lieber
title: Dallas mechanic exposes massive roofing scheme, police take the case - NewsBreak
text:
By Dave Lieber ,
9 hours ago Alvaro Lau Camarena of Euless is the leader of a movement to prosecute the roofer who allegedly stole half a million dollars from at least 40 customers. Alvaro is photographed in his Euless, Texas home office where he does his research, April 7, 2026. The roofer’s, Gilad Rubinsky, Collin County mugshot is posted (top) and a photo of Gilad and a friend (left) and a screenshot of him competing in the World Series of Poker last year (right). (Tom Fox/The Dallas Morning News) A 32-year-old aircraft mechanic from Dallas helped unravel the scheme of a notorious North Texas roofer accused of taking $500,000 in insurance payouts from about 40 customers without completing the promised work.
While customers were left without roofs—and without answers—the mechanic built a case of his own. Instead of hammers and nails, he used a spreadsheet and an online chat group to track victims across a dozen cities, compiling names, contact information, and reported losses.
Gilad Rubinsky is the roofer, and his nemesis is Alvaro Lau Camarena of Euless.
Lau Camarena’s spreadsheet is significant because it indicates a stark pattern of roofing fraud. Forty names are on the list with victims losing $1,500 to $50,000.
Each has something in common besides their loss. Victims signed over their insurance checks to Rubinsky’s company before work started. Consumer advocates say insurance checks should never get signed over until a job is completed.
This episode, which is still playing out, is one more glaring example of what’s wrong with the crooked roofing industry in the Lone Scam State.
For more than 20 years, The Watchdog has complained that without proper oversight it’s too easy for bad roofers to take the money and run.
Yet Gov. Greg Abbott and state lawmakers have refused to create either a licensing or registration system to give consumers some protection.
Often, city police departments hesitate to track down multiple victims of fraud. But when a citizen like Lau Camarena brings in such a complete listing of victims, it’s hard to say no.
Detectives from several cities have met to plot strategy. Meanwhile, some of the victims say they believe the FBI has stepped in to work the case, too.
The FBI declined comment.
Nicknamed Grumpy Rubinsky’s nickname at Dallas poker halls is Grumpy, a handle he picked up from his fellow poker players, said Chris Coles, a self-described professional poker player.
Coles, who according to the spreadsheet lost $38,651, said he believes poker losses was one of the reasons the roofer’s life took a downturn.
“I watched him lose time after time,” said Coles, who hired Rubinsky after meeting him at the poker table.
Rubinsky didn’t respond to requests for his side of this story.
A $50,000 loss The biggest loser on the lengthy list is Brad Welcher of Dallas, who reported a $50,000 loss.
“I made many, many mistakes here that I realize now,” he said. “I thought I was doing everything right. I did my due diligence on this guy, but I obviously did not. Me and all these people made huge mistakes.”
When the $50,000 insurance check arrived, Welcher told me that company sales rep Manjit Kapri told him it would be best if the company held the check to keep it safe. After that, Welcher never saw either the money or a new roof.
Kapri, who was fired by Rubinsky after five years working together, told me: “For 60 to 70 people we didn’t build a roof. We just collected the checks.”
How did they handle delays?
“Sometimes he would tell us to use the excuse of bad weather,” Kapri said. “Or they were waiting for a new crew.”
‘Not just me’ How did aircraft mechanic Lau Camarena build his spreadsheet? Painstakingly.
“I used Google reviews, Facebook and hashtags – whatever I could – and I started slowly building this group.” Kapri, the fired sales rep, helped him.
Lau Camarena’s campaign to expose Rubinsky took a sudden turn when he created the online chat room. Finally, victims had a place to meet.
When Gerson Santos of Dallas, who lost $8,584, found the chat room, he said, “Oh my goodness. It’s not just me. It’s a bunch of people.”
The chat room was therapeutic, allowing customers to share their stories and put the pieces of this puzzle together. They share documents, stories and even YouTube videos of the bearded Rubinsky wearing a blue baseball cap while playing in the Wide World of Poker.
Some believe the number of victims is larger than previously known. They fear that some Hispanic customers are afraid to come forward because of their immigration status.
Although a local police detective was invited into the chat room, he and others in law enforcement say they are chasing fraud, not citizenship.
Final words I reached out to Rubinsky and had about as much luck as his clients did. I sent emails to four email accounts associated with him and also three different phone lines, including two on his still-posted, live website.
Although Rubinsky didn’t talk to me, I heard him speak on voice mail messages he left for Coles, who played them for me.
In one message, he tried to make his position clear. “The fact that you gave me the check doesn’t mean that I made money. The check needs to build you a roof.”
He continued, “I do this since 2016 at the highest level. No one in this country understands roofing and the process better than I do. My goal is always to build quickly because that’s how I make money. That’s how I make my customers happy.”
